messages.subject_clean: Poke holes in my grand-theory CFA
messages.body_plain:
Jošt,

Right, the analogy of the dishes works correctly, in my opinion, except it is the way our genes behave, not the behavioral mechanism of our economical purchasing decisions of kitchen goods.  We prefer to reproduce more in dangerous environments, and we have no conscious idea of why we do that.  Within my perspective (and I generally recommend this perspective): EVERYTHING about the human species is biology.  If an objective phenomenon of the human species is not biology, then biology needs to be adjusted to accommodate that phenomenon.  The way social scientists tend to behave is that they bring in biology only if they must.  But I suggest the opposite: look outside biology only if you must.  You heard of the slur, "biological determinism."  What if we studied earthquakes, and, upon hearing any explanation grounded in standard geological models such as tectonic plates, we responded, "Oh, I would rather avoid geological determinism"?  Of course that would be ridiculous, and social scientists behave similarly with explanations for the human species, therefore failing to make proper sense of the human species, allowing autodidacts like me to fill in that knowledge vacuum.  That is great for me, but it is tragic for the social sciences, and it withholds from the whole human community the benefits of scientific progress.  You are a professional social scientist, so I suggest taking the necessary leap and breaking that spell.

Yours,

Abel

messages.body_plain:
Marzhan,
I am not a statistician but there is no inherent connection between data collection method (e.g. survey) and the appropriateness of SEM.  The salient data feature with SEM is typically the distribution.  When counts are large, into 3 digits, my understanding is that the normal distribution offers an adequate approximation to count data.  When counts are smaller, they follow a Poisson distribution and, like dichotomous data, the mean is not independent of the variance.  Also similar to dichotomous data, none of that really matters if the variable in question is exogenous because estimation is conditional on exogenous variables.  If you are not estimating mean structures and you use a robust estimator, that may suffice for an endogenous count variable with smaller counts.  You might also investigate whether a log transformation of a small count is of use.  Others may be able to elaborate, clarify or offer references.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Rose,
I think that your question is difficult to answer because it is not clear what question you wish to answer with your power study.  If it were me, I would probably be most interested in the power to detect the indirect effect as a defined parameter.  I would probably run separate conditions (separate calls to simsem()) for each of the three loading values.  I would probably generate the data sets within each condition based on a sequence of sample sizes from a minimum to a maximum with a specified length.  This would allow me to plot power against sample size, possibly using a smoothed line such as from the lowess() function.  I do not believe that there are any challenges specific to your model.  As such, you should be safe piecing together code borrowed from various examples in the tutorial.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
messages.subject_clean: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
messages.body_plain:
Rose,
Sorry, I let my Bayesian prior swamp the data and misread your question as being about mediation instead of moderation.

In the conversation that you cited, Terrence provides a script for simulating the latent interaction and Ed Rigdon provides sample code and a set of slides describing fitting the interaction model.  One strategy might be to follow Terrence's approach just for the indicators of the latent variables, not the interaction, and then use the semTools::inProd() or semTools::orthogonalize() to add the indicators of the interaction to the data set.  Both functions return a data set with the product indicators added to the original variables.  You could then return this augmented data set in your function passed to simsem as the data generation function.

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/PxFUKcIwPd0/m/-T67JNWL4doJ

If you have doubts about your code, the question is how can you test it.  One strategy would be to use your data generation function outside of simsem, call it on your own and save the data.  Then fit your interaction model to that data and evaluate the parameter recovery.  If you are able to recover the parameters that you used to generate the data, then that suggests that you are on the right track.  Use a large sample size to minimize sampling error for this test.  Choose effects that are clearly distinct from zero.

Terrence's code generates values for the latent variables.  You can leave these in your data without using them in your SE model.  You can plot the interaction using the simulated data to confirm that it looks the way you meant it to.

If your code passes these tests, then I would run a similar model through simsem and look at the mean parameter values across replications, again evaluating these for parameter recovery.  If you can recover the parameters that you put in, that suggests that you have things set up properly.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Yves for the comprehensive answer and all the work you have done!

I was a bit occupied with other work but finally got around to testing this bit of code today. This definitely helped me a lot!

It is nice to hear that using the lavPredict function with these options gets me to my goal using CFA. I have seen some people save factor scores from EFA, too (I guess it is an option in SPSS, heh). I imagine this would be possible with lavaan by using the efa function and having output="lavaan"?

This is a kind of an aside, but I was wondering what does the "Empirical Bayes Modal" approach do in lavPredict? As I understand it, it is the default for lavPredict and when testing with Holzinger-Swineford data, it returns the same result as method="regression".

Regarding sam, I have to correct my earlier post regarding the Widaman & Revelle analysis using the "global" option as they ran both local and global analyses and I copied the wrong part.

Here is the code for their analysis using the local option (full code: https://osf.io/swef8):
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------#
#--- Method 3: Factor score regression with Bartlett and Croon's correction on ROUNDED scores ----#
#---           Using the LOCAL option with the SAM fitting function                               #
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------#
meth_03aa = '

         f1 =~ r06_paracomp + r07_sentcomp + r09_wordmean
         f2 =~ r10_addition + r12_countdot + r13_sccaps

         f1 ~  school
         f2 ~  school
         '

fitm03aa = sam(model = meth_03aa, data=all, sam.method = 'local', estimator = 'MLR')

But I believe this does not detract from your general point about what the sam function does. It is nice to hear more details about sam, definitely need to keep that in mind for more specific future analyses.

> lavPredict() to compute factor scores but with the (new) transform =
> TRUE argument. For example:
>
> library(lavaan)
> example(cfa)
> FS <- lavPredict(fit, transform = TRUE)
> round(cor(FS), 3)
> # compare to:
> lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")
>
> This will 'transform' the (by default 'regression') factor scores in
> such a way that the variance-covariance matrix of the factor scores will
> coincide with the model-implied variance-covariance matrix of the latent
> variables that you get from the CFA fit. In theory, when you use these
> transformed factor scores later in a regression, you should get unbiased
> point estimates (although the standard errors will be underestimated, as
> they the ignore the uncertainty that stems from the CFA model).
>
> > In Devlieger et al. (2016; 10.1177/0013164415607618), regression FSR,
> > Bartlett FSR, the bias avoiding method of Skrondal & Laake (2001), the
> > bias correcting method of Croon (2002) and SEM were compared. The result
> > in my understanding was that both regression and Bartlett were biased,
> > and, outside of SEM, the best option would be the Croon bias correcting
> > method with the new SE developed in the paper.
>
> Indeed. Although the SE formula that we described in that 2016 paper was
> somewhat limited. The better version is reported in the SAM paper (and
> is also what lavaan is using in the sam() function).
>
> > 1) My first question is how to analyze factor score indeterminacy to see
> > if it is low?
>
> If you look at the standardized factor loadings, then factor score
> indeterminacy will be low if the standardized factor loadings are close
> to 1.
>
> > I saw Widaman & Revelle use the sam function in their Thinking
> > thrice about sum scores paper (2022; 10.3758/s13428-022-01849-w) and
> > they describe it as such: /"We used the “local” option with the default
> > ML mapping matrix in the sam fitting function (see Rosseel & Loh, 2021),
> > which is equivalent to the Skrondal and Laake approach with Croon’s
> > correction and the recently derived SEs of parameter estimates."/
>
> I am not sure what Widaman & Revelle mean with "the Skrondal and Laake
> approach". If they just refer to the generic idea of using factor scores
> in a regression, all is fine. But if they think that sam() uses Bartlett
> factor scores for 'endogenous' factors, and regression factor scores for
> 'exogenous' factors, then they are mistaken. The sam() function will in
> fact not even compute factor scores (explicitly). Local sam directly
> computes an estimate of the variance-covariance matrix of the latent
> variables, and uses that as input for a path-analysis or regression
> analysis in a second step.
>
> > fitm03b = sam(model = meth_03b, data=all, sam.method = 'global',
> > estimator = 'ML')
>
> Note that this is global sam, not local sam! Global sam first fits the
> CFA part, then plugs in all the parameters in the full model, and then
> estimates the remaining parameters of the structural part while keeping
> the measurement parameters fixed.
>
> > 2) My second question is two-fold: is the use of the sam function in
> > this manner really equivalent to Skrondal & Laake with Croon correction
> > and the new SEs?
>
> No, that is a misunderstanding. The sam() function does not work with
> factor scores... It works with 'summary statistics' (i.e., the mean
> vector and especially the variance-covariance matrix) of the latent
> variables.
>
> > If so, is there any way to get factor scores using the
> > Croon correction out of the sam function using just the measurement
> > part?
>
> No.
>
> But you can follow the method I described at the beginning to get what
> (I believe) you want: fit a CFA model with all factors included, and
> then use lavPredict(fit, transform = TRUE).
>
>
> Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

I've put together a script for simulating a moderation model using indProd and would appreciate your review (please!)
Model overview: Three latent variables, each with five indicators. Factor loadings: Set at 0.65 for each indicator. Regression coefficients for f3: 0.3 from f1 0.3 from f2 0.1 for the interaction between f1 and f2. I've structured the script to easily adjust factor loadings, coefficients, and to evaluate the power of these regressions. Could you confirm if this approach effectively assesses the power for the specified regression effects?
I will also adjust nrep and N.

Thank you for your expertise!
Rose

# Function to simulate data with a specific structure of interaction
SEM_sim_with_interaction <- function(N, FL, coefs) {

  # Calculate the error variance from the given factor loadings (FL)
  errorVar <- 1 - FL^2

  # Define the names for latent factors and manifest variables
  factorNames <- paste0("f", 1:3)
  manifestNames <- paste0("y", 1:15)

  # Construct a factor loading matrix (Lambda) with zeros, then fill in given loadings
  Lambda <- matrix(0, nrow = length(manifestNames), ncol = length(factorNames),
                   dimnames = list(manifestNames, factorNames))
  Lambda[1:5, 1] <- FL
  Lambda[6:10, 2] <- FL
  Lambda[11:15, 3] <- FL

  # Define the error variance-covariance matrix (Theta) for manifest variables
  Theta <- matrix(0, nrow = length(manifestNames), ncol = length(manifestNames),
                  dimnames = list(manifestNames, manifestNames))
  diag(Theta) <- c(rep(errorVar[1], 5), rep(errorVar[2], 5), rep(errorVar[3], 5))

  # Define the mean structure for the latent factors
  Alpha <- rep(0, length(factorNames))
  Tau <- rep(0, length(manifestNames))
  Mu <- Tau + Lambda %*% Alpha

  # Define the covariance matrix (Phi) for the first two common latent factors
  Phi <- matrix(1, nrow = 2, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(c("f1", "f2"), c("f1", "f2")))
  Phi[2, 1] <- .4
  Phi[1, 2] <- Phi[2, 1]

  # Generate multivariate normal data
  Kappa <- Alpha[1:nrow(Phi)]
  factors <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu = Kappa, Sigma = Phi))

  # Calculate the third endogenous latent factor using the coefficients (coefs)
  int3 <- Alpha[3]
  factors$f3 <- int3 + coefs[1]*factors$f1 + coefs[2]*factors$f2 + coefs[3]*factors$f1*factors$f2
  resVar <- 1 - var(factors$f3)
  factors$f3 <- factors$f3 + rnorm(N, sd = sqrt(resVar))

  # Generate unique factor data for manifest variables
  uniqueFactors <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu = Mu, Sigma = Theta))

  # Compute the manifest variables by combining common and unique factors
  manifests <- (as.matrix(factors) %*% t(Lambda)) + uniqueFactors

  # Create interaction terms for manifest variables using the indProd function
  interaction_data <- indProd(manifests,
                              var1 = c("y1", "y2", "y3", "y4", "y5"),
                              var2 = c("y6", "y7", "y8", "y9", "y10"),
                              doubleMC = TRUE, match = TRUE)

  # Return the combined dataset with manifest variables and their interactions
  return(cbind(manifests, interaction_data))
}

# Structural equation model
mod <- '
  # Define latent variables from manifest variables
    f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
    f2 =~ y6 + y7 + y8 + y9 + y10
    f3 =~ y11 + y12 + y13 + y14 + y15

   # Specify interaction terms for the latent variable
    f_int =~ y1.y6 + y2.y7 + y3.y8 + y4.y9 + y5.y10

  # Regression relations among latent variables
    f3 ~ c1*f1 + c2*f2 + c3*f_int
'

# Simulation based on the defined model
Output <- sim(5, model=mod, n=200,
              # 'FL=rep(.65, 5)' specifies that all factor loadings are set to .65 for each of the 5 manifest variables for each latent factor.
              # 'coefs = c(.3,.3,.1)' sets the regression coefficients for the components used to compute f3:
              # - coefs[1] = .3: coefficient for the relationship between f1 and f3 (coefs[1]*factors$f1)
              # - coefs[2] = .3: coefficient for the relationship between f2 and f3 (coefs[2]*factors$f2)
              # - coefs[3] = .1: coefficient for the interaction effect between f1 and f2 on f3 (coefs[3]*factors$f1*factors$f2).
              generate=function(n) SEM_sim_with_interaction(n,
                                                            FL=rep(.65, 5),
                                                            coefs = c(.3,.3,.1)),
              std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,
              lavaanfun = "sem",
              seed = 4523)

summary(Output)

> Rose,
> Sorry, I let my Bayesian prior swamp the data and misread your question as being about mediation instead of moderation.
>
> In the conversation that you cited, Terrence provides a script for simulating the latent interaction and Ed Rigdon provides sample code and a set of slides describing fitting the interaction model.  One strategy might be to follow Terrence's approach just for the indicators of the latent variables, not the interaction, and then use the semTools::inProd() or semTools::orthogonalize() to add the indicators of the interaction to the data set.  Both functions return a data set with the product indicators added to the original variables.  You could then return this augmented data set in your function passed to simsem as the data generation function.

> If you have doubts about your code, the question is how can you test it.  One strategy would be to use your data generation function outside of simsem, call it on your own and save the data.  Then fit your interaction model to that data and evaluate the parameter recovery.  If you are able to recover the parameters that you used to generate the data, then that suggests that you are on the right track.  Use a large sample size to minimize sampling error for this test.  Choose effects that are clearly distinct from zero.
>

>
> If your code passes these tests, then I would run a similar model through simsem and look at the mean parameter values across replications, again evaluating these for parameter recovery.  If you can recover the parameters that you put in, that suggests that you have things set up properly.

messages.subject_clean: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
messages.body_plain:
Rose,
I like you coding style, it is easy to read.  I especially liked the use of the anonymous function to pass parameters to the generate parameter to the sim() function.  I tend to use two-space indentation, following Google R coding style, but I found the single indent perfectly readable.

Your code ran for me and I did not catch any red flags.

5 replications with n=200 is not idea to evaluate parameter recovery.  The mean estimates seem plausible, but one thing that you could do is to run this with a very large sample size fore the sole purpose of evaluating parameter recovery as a means of checking your code.  I don't think that we should ever treat code review as a substitute for code testing.

I had to think about this for a moment but my understanding is that you are fine simulating variables with unit variances and analyzing them with analysis of covariance structure, you would only get into trouble if you standardize the data to force it into a correlation matrix and then analyze it as a covariance matrix, because you would then be treating fixed variances as random.  So, I think that simulating unit variances was a reasonable and safe strategy to simplify the code.  But if you want to maximize the similarity between your power study and the planned analysis, you might consider simulating data based on the observed or anticipated descriptive statistics.

The basic output gives you empirical standard errors.  However, if you are not already aware, simsem offers a number of ancillary functions specific to power studies.  I used the basic getPower() function which showed considerable variability in power cross the parameters of interest (not too surprising with N = 200).

My usual practice is to test the model specification with simulateData() before using it with sim() but I suppose you could accomplish much the same thing with a single replication using the draw() and exportData() functions.  (I have never done that.)  However, if the list of parameters in the sim() ouptut lines up with what you were expecting, your model specification is probably fine.  Here is one convenient way to count them: length(getPower(Output)).

One thing that I like to do, unrelated to the substance of your code, is to provide three-part internal documentation for any function: One line about the purpose of the function, one line about the parameters, and one line about the return value.  The middle line is especially helpful in R code because, to the best of my knowledge, there is no built in way to annotate the parameter types in the function definition syntax itself.  As an example of why this can be helpful, it was not immediately obvious to me whether FL was meant to be scalar or a vector until I read further into the code.

HTH,

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject_clean: What does exactly “sample.nobs” do in lavaan::sem?
messages.body_plain:
Hi alodie,

"sample.nobs" indicates the sample size. When you use the sample covariance matrix as input, you have to indicate the sample size separately, because it can't be inferred from the sample covariance matrix (which has the size p x p), but it's needed for the test statistics and model fit. In contrast, if you input data (which has the size N x p), then the sample size is inferred from the number of rows. (p = number of observed variables, N = sample size)

Best,
Julia

messages.subject: Multilevel SEM: lavaan sets negative variances in (sample) covariance matrix to 0
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel SEM: lavaan sets negative variances in (sample) covariance matrix to 0
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I noticed that in mulitlevel SEM, in the estimate of the between-group covariance matrix (Sigma_B) negative variances and related covariances  are set to 0. However, I did not find any information on this procedure in the official sources. Did I miss any sources? What is the reason for this procedure? I put a minimal example below.

Thanks in advance!

Best,
Julia

#######################

library(lavaan)
library(Morpho)
set.seed(1499)

# set population model (unstructured bivariate model)
Sigma_W <- "y ~~ 1*y;
            x ~~ 1*x;
            y ~~ 0.5*x"
Sigma_B <- "y ~~ 0.2*y;
            x ~~ 0.2*x;
            y ~~ 0.1*x"

# set sample sizes
n <- 4 # cluster size
g <- 5 # number of clusters

data_W <- simulateData(Sigma_W, sample.nobs=n*g, model.type="lavaan")
data_B <- simulateData(Sigma_B, sample.nobs=g, model.type="lavaan")
groups <- rep(1:g, each=n) # grouping variable
data_T <- data_W # create final total data matrix (that we would sample) in the following
data_T[,] <- 0
for (j in unique(groups)){
  for (i in min(which(groups == j)):max(which(groups == j)))
    data_T[i,] <- data_W[i,] + data_B[j,]
}
data_T$groups <- as.factor(groups)
data_T$persons <- rep(1:n, g)

# estimate model (same as population model)
model <- '
level: 1
y ~~ y
x ~~ x
y ~~ x
level: 2
y ~~ y
x ~~ x
y ~~ x
'
fit <- sem(model, data = data_T, cluster = "groups")

# estimate (sample) covariance matrices (I rebuild lavaans estimation of the between-group level sample covariance matrices here, see also Muthen 1989, 1990, 1994 for the estimators)
S_pw <- covW(data=data_T[,1:2], groups=data_T[,3])
group_means <- attr(S_pw, "means")
attr(S_pw, "means") <- NULL
grand_means <- colMeans(data_T[,1:2], na.rm = TRUE)
datac <- t(t(group_means) - grand_means)
S_B <- lavaan:::lav_matrix_crossprod(datac * n, datac)/(g - 1)
Sigma_B <- (S_B - S_pw) / n

# compare the Sigma_B
Sigma_B # Muthen (1989, 1990, 1994)
fit@SampleStats@YLp[[1]][[2]][["Sigma.B"]] # lavaan's implementation of Muthen (1989, 1990, 1994)

# the variance of x, and the related covariance xy, are set to zero in lavaan
#######################

References:
Muthén, B. O. (1989). Latent variable modeling in heterogeneous populations. Psychometrika, 54(4), 557–585. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02296397
Muthén, B. O. (1990). Mean and covariance structure analysis of hierarchical data. 88.
Muthén, B. O. (1994). Multilevel Covariance Structure Analysis. Sociological Methods & Research, 22(3), 376–398. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124194022003006

messages.subject: Re: What does exactly “sample.nobs” do in lavaan::sem?
messages.subject_clean: What does exactly “sample.nobs” do in lavaan::sem?
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

the sample size (N) is used to rescale the sample covariance matrix (S) because sample.cov.rescale=TRUE is the default (see in ?lavOptions). Lavaan uses the "biased" S without Bessel's correction (i.e., the denominator is N) and cov() is the "unbiased" S with Bessels' correction (i.e., the denominator is N-1). Rescaling the sample covariance matrix means multiplying it with *(N-1)/N because it is assumed that you give the "unbiased" S as input.

library(lavaan)
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

N <- nrow(HolzingerSwineford1939)

# unbiased S:
S_u <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)])
fit_u <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S_u, sample.nobs = N, sample.cov.rescale=FALSE)
lavInspect(fit_u, "sampstat") # same as S_u

# biased S:
S_b <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)])*(N-1)/N
fit_b <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S_b, sample.nobs = N, sample.cov.rescale=FALSE)
lavInspect(fit_b, "sampstat") # same as S_b

Irrespective of which estimator we use, we have to indicate the correct N to get correct test statistics and model fit statistics (correct as in not "cheating" with N and getting false statistics). I guess we can use robust standard error estimation with giving S as input though.
Further, I guess when "likelihood=wishart" then "sample.cov.rescale=FALSE" and thus the S we give as input is not changed by the N we indicate.

Hope that helps,

Best,
Julia

messages.subject_clean: Ordinal Data EFA - PML estimator takes too long
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Greetings. I am a newbie using lavaan here. I am using cfa() function to perform a CFA on ordinal data using the efa("efa")*f1 + efa("efa")*f2 + ... syntax based on the article here https://solomonkurz.netlify.app/blog/2021-05-11-yes-you-can-fit-an-exploratory-factor-analysis-with-lavaan/. I have around 527 observations with 146 variables.

By default, lavaan uses DWLS as the estimator running

lavaan::cfa(model = model_expression, data = df, rotation = "oblimin", ordered = TRUE)

It works fine but I was unable to compare models using AIC() and BIC() because DWLS is not ML-based.

So, I tried the pairwise ML as the estimator:

lavaan::cfa(model = model_expression, data = df, estimator = "PML", rotation = "oblimin", ordered = TRUE)

So far, the PML job has run for around 16 hours and is still running (compared to around 1 hour completion for the DWLS).

I am wondering if there is any tip to speed up the processing? Will multi-CPU help? Or using GPUs or other parallel processing?

Otherwise, is there another estimator in lavaan that allows me to use AIC() or BIC() with ordinal data?

Another question: According to https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/tutorial.pdf, page 29, at the very bottom of the page, it says " Full information maximum likelihood is currently not supported." for ordinal data, is that correct?

Thanks!

Regards,
Zhao

messages.subject: Re: Error in out$XX3.null : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
messages.subject_clean: Error in out$XX3.null : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure about this error, but I don't think your model is identified.

You have two first order factors, which have a covariance.

If you replace

mainfactor =~ factor1 + factor2

With

factor1 ~~ factor2

This model is equivalent to the model you want.

Your second order factor is trying to estimate two things (mainfactor's variance, and the loading of factor2) but it's only got one piece of information to do that with - and you can't estimate two things using one thing.

You can fix both loading to one.

mainfactor =~ 1 * factor1 + 1 * factor2

And then the variance of mainfactor will be equal (I think) to the covariance of factor1 and factor2 in the model I specified.

Hope that helps,

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Error in out$XX3.null : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
messages.subject_clean: Error in out$XX3.null : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
messages.body_plain:
I am not 100% certain but it may be a bug, or an error that is not detected.

In the source, if the computation of `out` (when computing CFI) leads to an error, `out` is supposed to be a try-error (due to the method, not a bug per se) that can be detected, and then you will not see the affected fit measures, without any error message.

However, in your case, it seems that somehow something's wrong in computing `out` but did not result in an error, resulting in the error message you received.

You can check whether it is due to fit measures by removing `fit.measures=T` when calling summary():

summary (early_ltask1_v2_fit,standardized=T)

If the error is due to fit measures computation, this should not result in an error (unless there are other issues).

You can also run this:

fitMeasures(early_ltask1_v2_fit, "cfi", output = "text")

This asks for *only* the CFI. My guess is, this will result in the same error message you received.

You may consider creating an issue at GitHub:

https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: Identification error when adding manifest predictor variable
messages.subject_clean: Identification error when adding manifest predictor variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Juliette.

I'm not sure if that's the problem, without something to reproduce the error, but I see some very big loadings and correlations in your model, which may indicate you have redundant variables and collinearity issues. So, when you add the predictor, there is at least one correlation/standardized loading higher than 1 (or less than -1).

My first step would see if there aren't any variables that I could drop/combine to decrease redundancy and/or try to constrain some parameters hoping this decreases the collinearity.

But there are many other things that could cause this error. E.g., when you added a new variable, you made your model more complex, and second-order models are already complex, so you need bigger samples.

Other people may notice something else, but I hope this can help you.

Best,
Yago

messages.subject: Power analysis using simsem: The correlation (RPS) matrix must be symmetric
messages.subject_clean: Power analysis using simsem: The correlation (RPS) matrix must be symmetric
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I would like to investigate power of a relatively straightforward mediation model using simsem. The model has two independent variables, one mediator, and one dependent variable, as can be seen in the figure attached.

Based on the recet paper by Donnelly, Jorgensen, and Rudolph (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01996-0), I tried to specify standardized regression parameters, with variance of exogenous variance fixed at 1 and correlation at .30 (an hypothetical value). To do so, I tried to specify the residual correlation as a PS matrix for the exogenous part, using the all-Y LISREL notation (which I used in the old days!).

However, this approach was incorrect, since I get the following error message:

Errore in buildModel(paramSet, modelType) :
  The correlation (RPS) matrix must be symmetric!

To my understanding, this is due to correlation between residuals of the two exogenous variables, but I was not able to find a solution (I tried the command symmetric = FALSE, but did not work).

You can see my syntax below, thanks for any advice.

Best,
Salvatore

***

#load simsem
library(simsem)

#set N
N <- 125

#set mediation parameters
a1 <- .30
a2 <- .30
b <- .30
c1 <- .10
c2 <- .10

#set beta.pop equal beta.free
beta.pop <- beta.free <- matrix(0, nrow = 4, ncol = 4, dimnames = list( c("Y","M", "X1", "X2"), c("Y","M", "X1", "X2")))

#Populate beta.free
beta.free["Y", "M"] <- "b"
beta.free["Y", "X1"] <- "c1"
beta.free["Y", "X2"] <- "c2"
beta.free["M", "X1"] <- "a1"
beta.free["M", "X2"] <- "a2"

#Populate beta.pop
beta.pop["Y", "M"] <- b
beta.pop["Y", "X1"] <- c1
beta.pop["Y", "X2"] <- c2
beta.pop["M", "X1"] <- a1
beta.pop["M", "X2"] <- a2

#Create SimMatrix
endoPaths <- bind(free = beta.free, popParam = beta.pop)

#Create correlation matrix of residuals
resid.pop <- resid.free <- matrix(0, nrow = 4, ncol = 4, dimnames = list(c("Y","M", "X1", "X2"), c("Y","M", "X1", "X2")))
resid.free[1,1] <- as.numeric(NA)
resid.free[2,2] <- as.numeric(NA)
resid.free[3,3] <- 1 #fixed at 1
resid.free[4,4] <- 1 #fixed at 1
resid.free[4,3] <- .3 #fixed at .3
resid.free[3,4] <- .3 #fixed at .3, try to fix the "RPS symmetric problem"
resid.pop <- diag(4)
resid.pop[4,3] <- .3
resid.pop[3,4] <- .3 #try to fix the "RPS symmetric problem"
residCor <- binds(free = resid.free, popParam = resid.pop, symmetric = FALSE)

#Set user parameters
userParams<-'
ind1 := a1*b
ind2 := a2*b
total1 := ind1+c1
total2 := ind2+c2
'

#Create SimSem model
simMod1 <- model.path(BE = endoPaths, RPS = residCor, con = userParams, indLab = rownames(beta.free))

Errore in buildModel(paramSet, modelType) :
  The correlation (RPS) matrix must be symmetric!

When looking at the @phiList, it appears as though the covariance matrices are accurate for all imputations. The error is as follows:

Error in PHI[[block.label[b]]] <- Reduce("+", lapply(phiList, "[[", i = b))/m :

 If I run each of the imputed datasets separately through compRelSEM I can get estimates. But I'm struggling with the pooled estimates.  Any help or guidance would be appreciated.

  Factor3 =~ physical1 + physical4+physical5

  # Factor covariances

messages.subject: Re: Extracting "residual terms" in CFA results
messages.subject_clean: Extracting "residual terms" in CFA results
messages.body_plain:
The criterion for choosing model parameters in OLS regression is minimizing (sum of squared) casewise residuals, but in SEM the criterion is minimizing residuals of summary statistics (covariance matrix: Sigma), not casewise/raw data.

Predicted / model-implied Sigma: lavInspect(fit, "cov.ov") or fitted(fit)
Observed Sigma(-hat) or S: lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")
Residuals = Predicted Sigma minus observed S: resid(fit) or more information from lavResiduals(fit)
You can use the lavPredictY() function to obtain casewise expected values, and you can manually calculate casewises residuals as the difference between casewise expected values and your raw data.  Jarrett Byrnes posted some example syntax in his feature request:

https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues/269

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Pooling factor scores across imputed data sets?
messages.subject_clean: Pooling factor scores across imputed data sets?
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan community,

 I would like to follow up on this question as I am
encountering a similar issue/question (tbh the issue relates to other threads
as well, however, I couldn’t come up with an “aggregate” solution). I am
attempting to fit a CFA with one latent factor, using a combination of
continuous and binary indicator variables. The dataset also contains missing
values. My objective is to obtain a factor score that I can subsequently use in
analyses to examine its relationship with disease progression—I am aware that this
is approach is debatable.

 Given the data characteristics, my preference was to
estimate the model WLSMV with multiple imputations. As a sanity check, I also
estimated the same model structure on the complete datasets for comparison, and
the results aligned well with each other. However, I am currently facing the
challenge of deriving factor scores, as plausible values and SEs appear to be
unattainable with models containing categorical data. Are there new solutions implemented in lavaan that I may not have come
across yet, or would I need to rely on blavaan for this (as here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/P5n1XILPo0M/m/n6u5EwgYBAAJ)?
I’m not yet experienced with this Bayesian approach and I would highly appreciate
some guidance.

 Another option I have been contemplating is the
aggregation of the categorical indicator variables, resulting in a risk factor
sum score—a widely used practice in my field. With this approach, I might be
able to transform the categorical indicators to exhibit continuous
characteristics. I could then address the missing data in the dataset using MLR/FIML
in the CFA when combining it with the other continuous indicators. However, at
present, this appears to be more of a "last resort" or compromise
solution.

 I would greatly appreciate any advice and suggestions.
Thank you in advance for your valuable feedback! If details are too hazy here,
I’m happy to provide more information of course.

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Donnerstag, 9. August 2018 um 09:49:11 UTC+2:
> > There are rules on how to pool parameters and standard errors with multiple imputations. I would see the factor scores as parameters, and you could follow those rules to pool them. For parameters, the pool factor score would be average across imputations.
>
> I would hesitate to see it that way unless factor scores are only linear functions of the parameters, in which case the average of transformation values is the same as transforming the average.  For instance, the fitted() and resid() methods for lavaan.mi objects do not simply average the model-implied moments or residuals across imputations, because those are not estimated parameters.  Instead, the model-implied moments and residuals are calculated from the pooled parameters, as they would be if using complete data (and those 2 methods do not yield the same result).
>
> I haven't written a predict() method for lavaan.mi objects because I don't support the use of treating factor scores as though they were observed values that can be used in a subsequent analysis.  Failing to take uncertainty of estimated factor scores into account yields biased SEs and test statistics, so error rates can be greatly inflated.  You can, however, adjust those SEs by using a 2-step estimation process.
>
> http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0013164415607618
>
> Yves is working on implementing that method in lavaan, but I think the new multilevel features are taking priority right now.  Once that is available, I would actually recommend using the 2-step factor-score regression analysis on each imputed data set, then pooling those estimates and (correct!) SEs and test statistics.  I would make sure runMI() can incorporate such an analysis, but I can't know when it would be available.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

c2 <- .10

beta.pop["M", "X1"] <- a1
beta.pop["M", "X2"] <- a2

#Create SimMatrix
endoPaths <- bind(free = beta.free, popParam = beta.pop)

#Create correlation matrix of residuals
resid.pop <- resid.free <- matrix(0, nrow = 4, ncol = 4, dimnames = list(c("Y","M", "X1", "X2"), c("Y","M", "X1", "X2")))

resid.free[2,2] <- as.numeric(NA)

resid.free[4,4] <- as.numeric(NA) #residuals variace exogenous variable freely estimated

#resid.pop <- diag(4)

residCor <- binds(free = resid.free, popParam = resid.pop)

#Set user parameters

ind1 := a1*b
ind2 := a2*b
total1 := ind1+c1
total2 := ind2+c2
'

#Create SimSem model
simMod1 <- model.path(BE = endoPaths, RPS = residCor, con = userParams, indLab = rownames(beta.free))

#Custom function to obtain
#MCCCIs for indirect effects
rejectMCCI <- function(object) {
CIs <- semTools::monteCarloCI(object)
apply(CIs, 1, function(CI) 0 < CI["ci.lower"] | 0 > CI["ci.upper"])
}

#Run simulatiom
#nRep should be 5000
out1<-sim(nRep=1000, model=simMod1, n=N, seed = 12345, outfun = rejectMCCI)

#Inspect nonconvergent replications
summary(out1)

#Get power,
summaryParam(out1, matchParam = TRUE, digits = 3)

#Empirical estimate of power for Monte Carlo CIs
testMCCI <- do.call(rbind, getExtraOutput(out1))
colMeans(testMCCI)

That's not very large, considering how many variables you are modeling.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/a0029315

Treating as numeric and using robust ML might not require as large a sample size for stable results.  Standardized parameters might still be slightly attenuated relative to assuming underlying normality of latent responses, but that isn't really a good basis for choosing whether to treat the responses as ordinal or numeric.

 https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2020.589965

>     The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)

>     does not appear to be positive definite!

No, you inspected the covariance matrix of variables.  The message is about the covariance matrix of parameter estimates.

ACOV <- vcov(fit.model)
cov2cor(ACOV) # any correlations near or in excess of 1?
det(ACOV) # etc.

>  should I change for MLM, robust and satorra.bentler?

That might be better, given the size of the model, but hard to know without a simulation tailored to your own situation.  How much larger would your sample be if you (multiply) imputed incomplete data?

Probably, given the small N relative to number of parameters.  The ratio is only around 5 for your hypothesized model, and is < 2 for your saturated model (the basis for calculating the model's chi-squared statistic).

messages.subject_clean: Comparing nested CFA models with ordered = TRUE
messages.body_plain:
> what's puzzling me is the output from lavTestLRT() with method = satorra.bentler.2010.  I thought that the method from that paper was simply offering a method to ensure that the test values are always positive

There is probably a mismatch with the default robust test you implicitly requested when treating data as ordinal.  The Satorra Bentler stats are mean-adjustments, but the default for DWLS estimation is a mean- and variance-adjusted statistic.  By default, lavTestLRT() will already select the "satorra.2000" method when it inspects your models.

> 1) I am sure I have recently seen a post here clarifying what tests lavaan uses for model comparisons when ordered = TRUE has been used with cfa() but I'm failing to find that and failing to search it up on the web.  Can someone point me to the details?

The Satorra (2000) paper is on the help page References, but the method currently employed is described here:

https://www.statmodel.com/download/WLSMV_new_chi21.pdf

> 2) Am I the only one who finds:
> ## lavaan NOTE:
> ##     The "Chisq" column contains standard test statistics, not the
> ##     robust test that should be reported per model. A robust difference
> ##     test is a function of two standard (not robust) statistics.
> a bit cryptic and fairly scary?!  I wonder if it could be expanded a bit to be clearer to non-experts?

You can find numerous posts on this forum from people who were scared because the Chisq diff column did not match the Chisq column.  This message was added to assuage that fear.  It just means what it says: You first calculate the difference between 2 non-robust chi-squared statistics (in the Chisq column), then robustify it (which appears in the Chisq diff column).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: compRelSEM(): how to name reliability coefficient in MTMM approach?
messages.subject_clean: compRelSEM(): how to name reliability coefficient in MTMM approach?
messages.body_plain:
Because you only define your trait factors (letting your method variance be captured by residual covariances), you can only calculate "omega hierarchical" to define each trait's composite reliability.  That is the proportion of the composite's variance that is attributable to individual differences on the trait itself.  Each trait's (hierarchical) reliability should be returned in your compRelSEM() call.

Omega "total" is the proportion of a composite's variance that is due to both trait and method factors.  This aligns more closely with traditional definitions of reliability, which consider all reliable variance (even non-target variance).  If you are interested in obtaining omega total, you would have to fit a statistically equivalent model that defines 7 method factors for the 7 "eocd" indicator sets that you use.  Those factors should be orthogonal to (uncorrelated with) the trait factors, and in many cases you would also want method factors to be orthogonal to each other (at the very least, to prevent empirical underidentification).  Your correlated residuals imply uncorrelated method factors, so the model would be statistically equivalent (i.e., for each method, you estimate 3 factor loadings instead of 3 residual covariances).
To obtain omega total for each trait's composite, you would need to call compRelSEM() once for each trait factor by adding the other 2 traits to the omit.factors= argument and setting return.total=TRUE.  Omega total would be labeled "total" in the output.

## omega total for Aut
compRelSEM(fit.modelo, tau.eq = FALSE , ord.scale = TRUE,
           omit.factors = c("Con","Imp"), return.total = TRUE)
## omega total for Con
compRelSEM(fit.modelo, tau.eq = FALSE , ord.scale = TRUE,
           omit.factors = c("Aut","Imp"), return.total = TRUE)
## omega total for Imp
compRelSEM(fit.modelo, tau.eq = FALSE , ord.scale = TRUE,
           omit.factors = c("Aut","Con"), return.total = TRUE)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Inga,

if you have access to Stata, you can do your analysis as a combination of -mi- for missing value imputation / plausible values, and -gsem- for modelling of any type of response data.

Doing Bayesian stuff properly takes two semester of graduate statistics to understand what's going on. Of course you always throw your data and your syntax into a black box, and with some luck you will get some numbers in the output. But there is a fair amount of both fine-tuning the MCMC algorithms and diagnostics that has to be done for the answers to be trustworthy. Importantly, proper Bayesian computing produces convergence red flags with multiple imputations / plausible values... because it wants to see infinitely many draws rather than 5 draws. So things are not what they seem.

messages.subject: MIMIC modelling for Informal Economy
messages.subject_clean: MIMIC modelling for Informal Economy
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I used the lavaan library to develop my MIMIC models to estimate Informal Economy values. I believe you may be familiar with the modelling, using a structural model to explain Informal Economy as a result of causal variables, and using a Measurement Model to have IE impacting some indicator variables.

Usually, MIMIC modelling for IE encompasses endogeneity, in the sense of having GPD variables as both causal and indicator variables.

On my modelling with MIMIC, I'm using inequality (GINI) as a causal variable. It's an endogenous variable, as inequality has impact on Informal Economy, and Informal Economy impacts inequality. The model was built this way on purpose, and my thesis is to show that the impact of inequality in Latin America is higher than in another sample of countries, e.g., worldwide sample.

MIMIC seemed to me the right tool to the modelling, exactly because of the way it's conceived.

Wanted to get your thoughts on it, as a reviewer of my article is questioning whether I shall use an endogenous variable on my MIMIC model. Literature has been using GDP as causal as well, and GDP is too endogenous.

Any light you may give me will be of help.

Thanks,

Marcos

messages.subject: Re: Multilevel SEM: lavaan sets negative variances in (sample) covariance matrix to 0
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel SEM: lavaan sets negative variances in (sample) covariance matrix to 0
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your answer, Terrence! :)

I summarize what I found/inferred:

The default in multilevel SEM is the quasi-Newton algorithm (QN, p. 137), which I also used in my example. When θ_B (between-level residual variances which may be comparable with between-level variances in the unstructured model in my example) is negative, non-convergence might occur, but “lavaan does not restrict θ_B estimates to be positive when using QN” (p. 138). Thus, I assume that lavaans dealing with negative variances at the between-level have changed by now, and that negative variances are set to 0 to prevent non-convergence issues (similar to the procedure in MPLUS, see p. 138).

Further, I assume that this procedure has nothing to do with positive definiteness. When negative variances and related covariances are set to 0, this does not yield a positive definite covariance matrix. It only prevents a matrix that has only negative or negative and zero eigenvalues (i.e., is negative semi-definite). Thus, matrices can be positive definite, positive-semi definite and indefinite. Further, according to the paper only the EM algorithm requires a positive definite between-level model-implied covariance matrix (p. 138).

Best,
Julia

> whether we can have ordinal data at the individual level and only continuous data at the second level, or if BOTH levels must only have continuous data.

Only continuous variables are supported for MLSEM.

> Is this possible with lavaan

lavaan only supports 2-level MLSEMs.  The only way to incorporate a third level is in wide format, like a growth curve model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen    (he, him, his)

messages.body_plain:
When collapsing two adjacent response categories, would you do this (a) for only the item that has the empty response category or (b) for all items (i.e., even for those that contain no empty response categories)?

In my case, only 1 item (out of 36 five-point Likert items with a possible range of 0 to 4) has no responses of 0. I am conducting EFA on these items with efa(estimator = "WLSMV") given that some items are heavily skewed.

Thanks!

Jeremy

> Hi again, Terrence.
>

> Best regards,
>
> Carlos
>
> Em sex, 28 de set de 2018 às 13:01, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> escreveu:
> > > I don't understand these messages well.
> >
> > The first two are the same message (printed once for the hypothesized model and once for the baseline model used for CFI, TLI), just providing information about other pooling options.  You can ignore them, but if you want to pass those arguments, you can.
> >
> > > Also, it seems that fitMeasures() does not accept the arguments test and pool.robust.
> >
> > You can, I just forgot to document in class?lavaan.mi that fitMeasures() has the "..." argument to pass arguments to lavTestLRT(.mi)
> >
> > > I have the following doubts: how does fitMeasures() pool the cfi, rmsea and srmr that are needed for the invariance tests?
> >
> > It applies the complete-data formulas to the pooled chi-squared (and pooled baseline-model chi-squared for incremental indices) for any chi-squared-based fit index.  For (S)RMR, it applies the complete-data formulas to observed and model-implied moments based on pooled parameter estimates.
> >
> > > Which fit measures can be pooled and which cannot?
> > > (I read this paper on using imputation in regression models:
> > >
> > > https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/sim.4067 <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fonlinelibrary.wiley.com%2Fdoi%2Ffull%2F10.1002%2Fsim.4067&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNE6niO-Kblhjo8zEnoEzzZxd7-Spw>
> > >
> > > which states that some statistics can be combined using Rubin's rules, but others cannot).
> >
> > Correct, although their Table VIII only asserts that a model's chi-squared/LRT statistic cannot be pooled because it is not an estimate of a parameter, so Rubin's rules for pooling estimates does not apply.  But they can be pooled using different methods, as documented on the ?lavTestLRT.mi help page.
> >
> > Regarding the SRMR, the differences between observed and model-implied moments are also NOT estimated parameters, but rather functions of parameters.
> > The observed moments can be considered the parameter estimates of the saturated model (which is used to calculate the model's chi-squared/LRT statistic). So the pooled observed moments are simply the average of the sample statistics in each imputation.
> > The model-implied moments are not estimated parameters, but are functions of the estimated model parameters.  So the pooled model-implied moments are calculated the same way they are for complete data, but using the pooled parameter estimates.  In other words, this is the "sensible transformation before combination" they mention in their Table VIII.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
We are facing some issues conducting CFA with the lavaan package and hoped some of you might be able to help.

Context:
We are conducting a French validation study of a questionnaire (which already exists in English) that measures some features of a given behavior (e.g., awareness, controlability). It is composed of 11 or 12-items depending on its version and responses are made on 7-point Likert scales. The behavior to focus on is specified by the experimenter and can vary from study to study (e.g., some researchers might want to explore the features of smoking a cigarette whereas others might want to explore the ones of running).

We have recruited more than 500 participants for this study, who were divided into 6 subgroups that have to focus on different behaviors to respond to the questionnaire (e.g., washing hands, drinking coffee)

EFA conducted on previous studies revealed that a 3-factor solution might be suited to the data of the 11 and 12-iems versions of this questionnaire. An EFA conducted in this study, with the entire sample, also revealed that a 3-factor solution might be suited to the data, but some items are not loaded on the same factor as previously.

We have performed CFA with the entire sample regarding a one-factor model, a first 3-factor higher-order model and a first hierarchical model (based on EFA of previous studies) as well as alternative 3-factor higher-order and hierarchical models (based on EFA of this study). There was no particular problem with those analyses. However, we try to reproduce them on each subgroup and are sometimes receiving a warning "fit measures not available if model did not converge" and sometimes receiving a warning "computation of robust CFI / RMSEA failed". We would need some help to fix it.

It might be important to add two general information:
1) The EFA of this study indicates that some items loaded significantly on more than one factor.
2) Based on previous posts on this topic, we have checked the variance of each items and factors and none of them were null.

You’ll find below further information on each warning signal:

“Fit measure not available if model did not converge”
This type of warning seems to appear mainly for the higher-order model. It can appear for the 3-factor solution that is based on EFA of previous studies and not with the one that is based on EFA of this study; but also the contrary ; or both.
In each case this warning is present, it appears that the latent variable estimate of one of the three factors is especially high compared to the two other ones (e.g., 300 vs 1 or 2)

messages.subject: Re: CFA warning : model did not converge ; computation of robust CFI / RMSEA failed
messages.subject_clean: CFA warning : model did not converge ; computation of robust CFI / RMSEA failed
messages.body_plain:
I think this is an example of a "nearly not identified" model. Statistical identification has to do with whether one unique best solution exists for a model's parameters, given data and estimator. But this is not a 0 / 1 decision. Identification can hinge on whether a given parameter is "large" or is "near 0," with "large" and "near" being matters of degree. The small sample sizes for the individual behaviors make this situation more likely in your case.

Other elements that make an identification problem more likely in your case are using a higher order factor model with only 3 first order factors and the inclusion of free residual covariances in a factor model with not too many observed variables per factor. For the second order factor model to be statistically identified, the three first order factors must all load strongly on it--with a higher bar here given the low sample size. If any one loading is low, identification can fail. My first suggestion is to set aside the higher order factor structure until you resolve any other problems. A simple correlated factors model will be empirically identical to the higehr order factor model, in your situation, but will b e less prone to identification problems.

In addition, the "Repetition" factor has only 3 indicators, and two of those have free residual covariances. The free residual covariances make the identification of the Repetition factor doubtful, and this might be the core problem. Notice the near-zero loadings on that factor. (Unstandardized parameter estimates can be hard to interpret, but your factors have variances of 1, and your indicators have finite variances given that they come from 7 point Likert type scales.) So you might also try estimating a model without the residual covariances relating to Q1Freq and Q12Lgtps, to see if that will lead to a converged solution.

Combining responses regarding different behaviors may be inappropriate. This fixed coefficient model assumes all parameters have equal values across all respondents. If parameters vary across behaviors, then the output from the combined sampels may not be a good guide to what you will get from separate subsamples.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Clare,

I don't know the 'mediation literature' very well, and perhaps a 'good
practice' for this setting has been described elsewhere.

But I don't see an easy solution. I would try to find a numerical coding
for the ordinal variable (m) that is realistic (perhaps simply 1,2,3;
but maybe 1,2,5 is better; you can also center: -1,0,1) and then treat m
as pseudo-continuous. That would at least allow you to create the
interaction term.

If the interaction is important, then ignoring this interaction term
seems more harmful to me than treating an ordinal variable as continuous.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Mediation + Moderation w/ an ordered multicategorical var in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Mediation + Moderation w/ an ordered multicategorical var in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would start by thinking really hard if you need a nonlinear model for m and if you can assume interval scaling of m when used it as a predictor. If yes to both questions, you can use lavaan for the analysis. Regression diagnostics (residual-vs-fited plots, added variable plots) should give you some indication.

If either of these assumptions fail, lavaan is not the right tool for the job. Instead, I would recommend the mediation package, which does nonlinear mediation models.

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mediation/vignettes/mediation.pdf

For an explanation of what these nonlinear mediation models do, see

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IaPmGw0xr60

and

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ama6EseGYho

The first video talks about the general idea of causal mediation and the second about applications to nonlinear models.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
# A Simulate data reflecting a bifactor Model (3 factors; 3 items per factor)
# A1. Set up the loading matrix
myfload <- matrix(c(round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), rep(0, 6),
                    rep(0,3), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), rep(0,3),
                    rep(0,6), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2), round(rnorm(1, 0.8, .1),2)),
                  ncol = 3)

# A2. Set up the correlation matrix for the three factors
a_a <- 1
a_b <- round(rnorm(1, +.1, .05),2);
a_c <- round(rnorm(1, -.3, .05),2)
b_b <-1
b_c <- round(rnorm(1, +.1, .05),2)
c_c <-1
myphi <- matrix(c( a_a, a_b, a_c,
                 a_b, b_b, b_c,
                 a_c, b_c, c_c), ncol=3)

# A3. Generate data with the above structure
myout <- simFA(Loadings =
                  list(FacPattern = myfload),
                Phi =
                  list(PhiType = "user",
                       UserPhi = myphi),
                Bifactor =
                  list(Bifactor = TRUE,
                       F1FactorRange = c(.3, 4),
                       F1FactorDist = "fixed"),
                FactorScores =
                  list(FS = TRUE,
                       Population = TRUE,
                       NFacScores = 300))

# A4. Get the data from the simulation
data1    <- data.frame(myout$Scores$Observed)

# A5. Get the factor scores from the simulation
Fscores1 <- data.frame(myout$Scores$FactorScores)

# A6. Add id numbers to merge the two datasets
data1$id <- 1:nrow(data1); Fscores1$id <- 1:nrow(Fscores1);

# A7. Merge the two dataset
df <- merge(data1, Fscores1, by.x="id")

# B. Lavaan Section
# B1. Lavaan perfectly replicates the bifactor model
library(lavaan)
m1 <- '
factor1 =~ X1 + X2 + X3
factor2 =~ X4 + X5 + X6
factor3 =~ X7 + X8 + X9
factorH =~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7 + X8 + X9
'
fit_m1 <- sem(m1, estimator="MLM",orthogonal=T, data=df)
summary(fit_m1, fit.measures=T, standardized=T)

# B2. Now assume that I create a dependent variable, called DV,  within the dataset
df$DV <- (.20*df$G)+(.20*df$F1) +(.00*df$F2)+(-.20*df$F3)+ rnorm(nrow(df), 0, 3)

# B3.  A Regression Model predicts the dependent variable as follows
m2a <- lm(DV ~ G + F1 + F2 + F3, data=df); summary(m2a)

# B4. The same model, through lavaan, fails to converge
m2b <- '
factor1 =~ X1 + X2 + X3
factor2 =~ X4 + X5 + X6
factor3 =~ X7 + X8 + X9
factorH =~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7 + X8 + X9
DV ~ factorH + factor1 + factor2 + factor3
'
fit_m2b <- sem(m2b, estimator="MLM",orthogonal=T, data=df)
summary(fit_m2b, fit.measures=T, standardized=T)

So, what am I missing here? Is there a way to get the model to converge?
I thank you for your consideration
Thanasis

messages.subject_clean: How are the starting values calculated in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Noell,

In lavaan 0.6-15, by default, the factor loadings are initialized using FABIN3 (Hägglund, 1982). The residual variances of the observed indicators are set to half of the observed variance, and the latent variances are set to 0.05. Covariances and regression coefficients are initialized to zero. So indeed, no random starting values are employed.

Kind Regards,
Julie

Hägglund, G. , (1982). Factor analysis by instrumental variables methods. Psychometrika, 47, 209–222

Some other meaningful starting values can come from say instrumental variable estimators (Bollen's long, long thread of contributions; I was fortunate to hop on that train of thought for a couple of those). I initialized my Stata -confa- CFA program (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1536867X0900900301) with the instrumental variable estimates (with semi-meaningful residual variances like half of the marginal variance), I have seen far more stable convergence than random starting values or zeroes. lavaan is open source... steal my idea and PR it and make yourself famous.

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)
-- Principal Statistician, NORC @NORCnews
-- Opinions stated in this email are mine only, and do not reflect the position of my employer
-- Social media: @StatStas [ Twitter | mastodon.online ]
-- http://stas.kolenikov.name

On Thu, Sep 21, 2023 at 9:33 AM Julie De Jonckere <juliede...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Noell,
>
> In lavaan 0.6-15, by default, the factor loadings are initialized using FABIN3 (Hägglund, 1982). The residual variances of the observed indicators are set to half of the observed variance, and the latent variances are set to 0.05. Covariances and regression coefficients are initialized to zero. So indeed, no random starting values are employed.
>
> Kind Regards,
> Julie
>
> Hägglund, G. , (1982). Factor analysis by instrumental variables methods. Psychometrika, 47, 209–222
>
> Op donderdag 21 september 2023 om 16:02:20 UTC+2 schreef Noell Röhrig:

> > I was wondering how the starting values of the likelihood function are calculated in R lavaan for ML Estimation. I have heard that most programs (e.g., LISREL) systematically choose their starting values (instead of randomly). Is this the case for R lavaan as well? If so, how are they calculated?
> >
> > Thanks in advance,
> > Noell
>

messages.subject: Pooling goodness of fit indices using semTools::runMI
messages.subject_clean: Pooling goodness of fit indices using semTools::runMI
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am conducting a confirmatory factor analysis on some survey (ordinal) data (range: 1-4). Given the presence of missing data, I am using semTools::runMI to generate multiple imputed datasets and pool the results using the Rubin's formula. However, as you can see below, the combined goodness of fit indices do not make much sense (CFI = 1, TLI > 1, RMSEA = 0, SRMR = 0.09), especially when compared to the goodness of fit indices estimated from each individual dataset. Does anybody know how to fix this issue? I thought I could take the average of the goodness of fit indices from the results associated with each imputed dataset, but there might be a better solution.

Other than this, I wonder if there is an easy way to add information about auxiliary variables (e.g., gender, linguistic background) to the runMI function to improve the imputation process.

R syntax:

ordered2 <- scaled_db_lib |> select(i1:i6, i8:i22, i25:i28) |> colnames()

out1 <- semTools::runMI(model_cfa,
                        data = scaled_db_lib_mice,
                        m = 5,
                        miPackage = "mice",
                        fun = "cfa",
                        rotation = "oblimin",
                        estimator = "WLSMV", ordered = ordered2)

#Pooled goodness of fit indices
> out1 |> fitMeasures(c("cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr"))
"D3" only available using maximum likelihood estimation. Changed test to "D2".
Robust corrections are made by pooling the naive chi-squared statistic across 5 imputations for which the model converged, then applying the average (across imputations) scaling factor and shift parameter to that pooled value.
To instead pool the robust test statistics, set test = "D2" and pool.robust = TRUE.

messages.subject: Measurement invariance not constraining residuals across groups
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance not constraining residuals across groups
messages.body_plain:
As similar to a previous conversation: "Measurement Invariance group.equal not constraining residuals"

I am also having a similar issue but I have used measeq.syntax, parameterisation theta, and constrained the thresholds. I won't write out my model, but it is a 9 correlated factor model.

scale←measEq.syntax(configural=Corfactor, data=data,

parameterization = “theta”, group = “Reporter”,

ordered=T, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,

group.equal=c(“loadings”, “thresholds”),

meanstructure =T)

scale<as.character(scale)

fit.scale←cfa(scale, data=data, group = “Reporter”, estimator=”WLSMV”, ordered=T)

strict←measEq.syntax(configural=Corfactor, data=data,

parameterization = “theta”, group = “Reporter”,

ordered=T, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T,

group.equal=c(“loadings”, “thresholds”, “residuals”),

meanstructure =T)

strict<as.character(strict)

fit.strict←cfa(strict, data=data, group = “Reporter”, estimator=”WLSMV”, ordered=T)

These models are very similar, with a slight increase in the degrees of freedom of the strict model, and the residuals don't appear to have been constrained. The names of the residual parameters are the same across the groups but the values are different.

messages.subject: Re: What does exactly “sample.nobs” do in lavaan::sem?
messages.subject_clean: What does exactly “sample.nobs” do in lavaan::sem?
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for all your responses. I now better understand how the covariance matrix is scaled with N.

Given that, is it safe to estimate the model with different Ns (e.g., 250, 500, 750, 1000 and 2000) in order to determine which sample size would have been the best to get stable results and estimates?
Only to be clear: The goal is not to "cheat". The goal is to simulate the best minimum sample size.

mountk...@gmail.com schrieb am Dienstag, 12. September 2023 um 23:29:15 UTC+2:
> Hi again,
>
> the sample size (N) is used to rescale the sample covariance matrix (S) because sample.cov.rescale=TRUE is the default (see in ?lavOptions). Lavaan uses the "biased" S without Bessel's correction (i.e., the denominator is N) and cov() is the "unbiased" S with Bessels' correction (i.e., the denominator is N-1). Rescaling the sample covariance matrix means multiplying it with *(N-1)/N because it is assumed that you give the "unbiased" S as input.
>
> library(lavaan)
> HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
> N <- nrow(HolzingerSwineford1939)
>
> # unbiased S:
> S_u <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)])
> fit_u <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S_u, sample.nobs = N, sample.cov.rescale=FALSE)
> lavInspect(fit_u, "sampstat") # same as S_u
>
> # biased S:
> S_b <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)])*(N-1)/N
> fit_b <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S_b, sample.nobs = N, sample.cov.rescale=FALSE)
> lavInspect(fit_b, "sampstat") # same as S_b
>
>
> Irrespective of which estimator we use, we have to indicate the correct N to get correct test statistics and model fit statistics (correct as in not "cheating" with N and getting false statistics). I guess we can use robust standard error estimation with giving S as input though.
> Further, I guess when "likelihood=wishart" then "sample.cov.rescale=FALSE" and thus the S we give as input is not changed by the N we indicate.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> Best,
> Julia
>
> shufai...@gmail.com schrieb am Dienstag, 12. September 2023 um 17:11:22 UTC+2:
> > If we add likelihood = "wishart" ,  the covariance matrix being analyzed will be the same:
> >
> > library(lavaan)
> > HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
> >               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
> >               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
> >
> > dat_cov <- cov(HolzingerSwineford1939[, paste0("x", 1:9)])
> >
> > fit <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 20, likelihood = "wishart")
> > (tmp1 <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat"))
> > fit <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 50, likelihood = "wishart")
> > (tmp2 <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat"))
> > fit <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 200, likelihood = "wishart")
> > (tmp3 <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat"))
> > fit <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = dat_cov, sample.nobs = 500, likelihood = "wishart")
> > (tmp4 <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat"))
> >
> > # Verify that the covariance matrices analyzed are the same
> > all.equal(tmp1, tmp2)
> > all.equal(tmp2, tmp3)
> > all.equal(tmp3, tmp4)
> > all.equal(dat_cov, unclass(tmp1$cov), ignore_attributes = TRUE)
> >
> > You can take a look at the sections "sample.cov.rescale" and "likelihood" in the help page of lavOptions.
> >
> > Hope this helps.
> >
> > -- Shu Fai

messages.subject: A strange behavior of equal()
messages.subject_clean: A strange behavior of equal()
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have never used equal() in mode syntax, as far as I can recall. Using labels is much more convenient. However, I am working on something that may require me to work with it, and I came across a strange behavior.

This is the example:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-16
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.

mod1 <-
"
x4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3
x5 ~ a * x1 + equal('x5 ~ x1') * x2
"

fit1 <- sem(mod1, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
parameterEstimates(fit1)[c(4, 5), ]
#>   lhs op rhs label   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 4  x5  ~  x1     a 0.306 0.064 4.798  0.000    0.181    0.430
#> 5  x5  ~  x2 x5~x1 0.063 0.063 0.993  0.321   -0.061    0.186

mod2 <-
"
x4 ~ x1 + x2 + x3
x5 ~ x1 + equal('x5 ~ x1') * x2
"

fit2 <- sem(mod2, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
parameterEstimates(fit2)[c(4, 5), ]
#>   lhs op rhs label   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 4  x5  ~  x1  .p4. 0.183 0.038 4.832      0    0.109    0.258
#> 5  x5  ~  x2 x5~x1 0.183 0.038 4.832      0    0.109    0.258
```

<sup>Created on 2023-09-24 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

In the first version, I expect  "x5 ~ a * x1 + equal('x5 ~ x1') * x2" will make the paths "x5 ~ x1" and "x5 ~ x2" equal. However, it is not the case, as shown in the parameter estimates.

If I remove the label, then equal() works as expected, as shown in the second version.

I checked the parameter tables:

Version 1:

   id lhs op rhs user block group free ustart exo label plabel  start   est
4   4  x5  ~  x1    1     1     1    4     NA   0     a   .p4.  0.306 0.306
5   5  x5  ~  x2    1     1     1    5     NA   0 x5~x1   .p5.  0.063 0.063

Version 2:

   id  lhs op  rhs user block group free ustart exo label plabel  start   est
4   4   x5  ~   x1    1     1     1    4     NA   0  .p4.   .p4.  0.306 0.183
5   5   x5  ~   x2    1     1     1    5     NA   0 x5~x1   .p5.  0.063 0.183
15 15 .p4. == .p5.    2     0     0    0     NA   0               0.000 0.000

In the first version, equal() added 'x5~x1' as a label to 'x5~x2'. However, if 'x5~x1' is also labelled manually, the equality constraint is not added.

Moreover, when I fitted the first version, there was no warning message.

I don't know whether this can be considered a bug. Or is equal() not intended to be used with labelled parameters? If this is the case, how about adding a warning message or even raising an error?

Regards,
Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: Creating lavaan syntax from a parameter table?
messages.subject_clean: Creating lavaan syntax from a parameter table?
messages.body_plain:
This thread (I started) is nearly two-year old ... and I finally wrote a function, ptable_to_syntax(), to do this in the package semhelpinghands: converting a parameter table back to a model syntax (not because I "have time" ... but because I need to do this in another project):

https://sfcheung.github.io/semhelpinghands/reference/ptable_to_syntax.html

As Terrence showed, it is not difficult if we just need to have a long list of lhs-op-rhs strings. I wrote this function to make the syntax more readable, hopefully, as this is what I need in that project.

As a safeguard, I also wrote a function to compare two parameter tables, to check whether the syntax can produce the same parameter table.

I shared it here, in case there are other lavaan users who would like to do this (very) unusual thing.

It is only in the GitHub version of the package for now as I won't submit a new version to CRAN until probably late October.

There are models that the function does not yet support, due to the complexity that is difficult to foresee. But what it supports now is enough for me.

I tried to be conservative and it should refuse to work on models I know it does not support. Nevertheless, if you encountered any bugs, I would love to know. Thanks.

-- Shu Fai

However, if I want to describe the updated/generated model in lavaan syntax/language in the same R markdown file, then I need to manually write the syntax in the same document. It would be great to have a function to read the parameter table and then generate the corresponding lavaan syntax, to reduce the chance for human error.

> > Certainly, with some clever, rather easy use of paste() along with ifelse() to check for a user-defined $label or fixed value per parameter.
> > You should know that you can specify each parameter on its own line (without using the + operator like so many examples), and that lavaan accepts a character vector that it collapses into a single string, so you would not have to paste(..., collapse="") it yourself.  You could certainly collect all righthand-side variables that share a lefthand side and operator, but if your goal is readability, it wouldn't always be prudent in models with many variables.

```
           ## x1 and x2 are correlated
           x1 ~~ ra*x2"

           ## Variances of x1 and x2 are 1
           x1 ~~ 1*x1
           x2 ~~ 1*x2
           ## x1 and x2 are correlated
           x1 ~~ rb*x2"
```
Much appreciated,
Simon

messages.subject: Re: lavaan syntax duplication
messages.subject_clean: lavaan syntax duplication
messages.body_plain:
No sure if this is what you need. The model syntax is just a string. So you can add a placeholder (e.g., !!suffix!!) and the change it to anything you need using gsub()

``` r
model0 <- "
y ~ b1!!suffix!!*x1 + b2!!suffix!!*x2

## Variances of x1 and x2 are 1
x1 ~~ 1*x1
x2 ~~ 1*x2
## x1 and x2 are correlated

x1 ~~ r!!suffix!!*x2
"

modela <- gsub("!!suffix!!", "a", model0, fixed = TRUE)
modelb <- gsub("!!suffix!!", "b", model0, fixed = TRUE)

cat(modela)
#>
#> y ~ b1a*x1 + b2a*x2
#> ## Variances of x1 and x2 are 1
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> ## x1 and x2 are correlated
#> x1 ~~ ra*x2
cat(modelb)
#>
#> y ~ b1b*x1 + b2b*x2
#> ## Variances of x1 and x2 are 1
#> x1 ~~ 1*x1
#> x2 ~~ 1*x2
#> ## x1 and x2 are correlated
#> x1 ~~ rb*x2
```

<sup>Created on 2023-09-27 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

On 9/24/23 02:58, Shu Fai Cheung wrote:
> x5 ~ a * x1 + equal('x5 ~ x1') * x2

This will fail indeed, as the 'a' label overwrites the 'automatic' label
'x5 ~ x1'. It would be nice indeed if this triggers a warning, but I
don't see how this can be done using the current implementation of the
syntax parser in lavaan (lavParseModelString()). Only the 'labels' are
saved, and afterwards, we cannot check which one was the result of equal().

Perhaps I should remove equal() altogether in a future update...

Yves.

messages.subject: Running time for different parameterization methods
messages.subject_clean: Running time for different parameterization methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
We have been running some models looking at measurement invariance of a bifactor model with ordinal data. We followed the approach of Wu and Estabrook (2016), using the semtools function. We have about 10,000 participants and 67 items in the model. When we run the model with theta parameterization it takes a very long time to complete. When we run the model with delta parameterization it is somewhat faster, but still takes a couple of hours. Also, the wisdom seems to be to go with theta parameterization. Model fit seems pretty good and there do not seem to be any major problems with model estimates.

What should I be looking for to try and speed up the model estimation?

Thanks in advance!

Burt
